[text-15] "The word duck comes from Old English dūce 'diver', a derivative of the verb *dūcan 'to duck, bend down low as if to get under something, or dive', because of the way many species in the dabbling duck group feed by upending; compare with Dutch duiken and German tauchen 'to dive'."
[text-16] "Pacific black duck displaying the characteristic upending \"duck\""
[text-17] "This word replaced Old English ened /ænid 'duck', possibly to avoid confusion with other words, such as ende 'end' with similar forms. Other Germanic languages still have similar words for duck, for example, Dutch eend, German Ente and Norwegian and. The word ened /ænid was inherited from Proto-Indo"
[text-18] "A duckling is a young duck in downy plumage[1] or baby duck,[2] but in the food trade a young domestic duck which has just reached adult size and bulk and its meat is still fully tender, is sometimes labelled as a duckling."
[text-19] "A male is called a drake and the female is called a duck, or in ornithology a hen.[3][4]"
[text-20] heading "Taxonomy"
[text-21] "All ducks belong to the biological order Anseriformes, a group that contains the ducks, geese and swans, as well as the screamers, and the magpie goose.[5] All except the screamers belong to the biological family Anatidae.[5] Within the family, ducks are split into a variety of subfamilies and 'trib"
[text-22] "In most modern classifications, the so-called 'true ducks' belong to the subfamily Anatinae, which is further split into a varying number of tribes.[10] The largest of these, the Anatini, contains the 'dabbling' or 'river' ducks – named for their method of feeding primarily at the surface of fresh w"
[text-23] "A number of other species called ducks are not considered to be 'true ducks', and are typically placed in other subfamilies or tribes. The whistling ducks are assigned either to a tribe (Dendrocygnini) in the subfamily Anatinae or the subfamily Anserinae,[15] or to their own subfamily (Dendrocygnina"
[text-24] heading "Morphology"
[text-25] table row " | This section does not cite any sources. Please help improve this section by adding citations to reliable sources. Unsourced material may be challenged and removed. (October 2024) (Learn how and when to remove this message)"
[text-26] "The overall body plan of ducks is elongated and broad, and they are also relatively long-necked, albeit not as long-necked as the geese and swans. The body shape of diving ducks varies somewhat from this in being more rounded. The bill is usually broad and contains serrated pectens, which are partic"
[text-27] "The drakes of northern species often have extravagant plumage, but that is moulted in summer to give a more female-like appearance, the \"eclipse\" plumage. Southern resident species typically show less sexual dimorphism, although there are exceptions such as the paradise shelduck of New Zealand, whic"
[text-28] heading "Distribution and habitat"
[text-29] "See also: List of Anseriformes by population"
[text-30] "Flying steamer ducks in Ushuaia, Argentina"
[text-31] "Ducks have a cosmopolitan distribution, and are found on every continent except Antarctica.[5] Several species manage to live on subantarctic islands, including South Georgia and the Auckland Islands.[21] Ducks have reached a number of isolated oceanic islands, including the Hawaiian Islands, Micron"
[text-32] "Some duck species, mainly those breeding in the temperate and Arctic Northern Hemisphere, are migratory; those in the tropics are generally not. Some ducks, particularly in Australia where rainfall is erratic, are nomadic, seeking out the temporary lakes and pools that form after localised heavy rai"
[text-33] heading "Behaviour"
[text-34] heading "Feeding"
[text-35] "Ducks eat food sources such as grasses, aquatic plants, fish, insects, small amphibians, worms, and small molluscs."
[text-36] "Dabbling ducks feed on the surface of water or on land, or as deep as they can reach by up-ending without completely submerging.[25] Along the edge of the bill, there is a comb-like structure called a pecten. This strains the water squirting from the side of the bill and traps any food. The pecten i"
[text-37] "Diving ducks and sea ducks forage deep underwater. To be able to submerge more easily, the diving ducks are heavier than dabbling ducks, and therefore have more difficulty taking off to fly."
[text-38] "A few specialized species such as the mergansers are adapted to catch and swallow large fish."
[text-39] "The others have the characteristic wide flat bill adapted to dredging-type jobs such as pulling up waterweed, pulling worms and small molluscs out of mud, searching for insect larvae, and bulk jobs such as dredging out, holding, turning head first, and swallowing a squirming frog. To avoid injury wh"
[text-40] "The Guardian published an article advising that ducks should not be fed with bread because it damages the health of the ducks and pollutes waterways.[26]"
[text-41] "Sandra C. Mitchell, DVM, DABVP suggests, with water: small fish, snails, crabs, insects, slugs, chopped lettuce, chopped cabbage, cracked corn, sliced grapes, frozen peas, cooked oats, cooked rice, grass seed, or commercial duck feed.[27]"
[text-42] heading "Breeding"
[text-43] "Ducks generally only have one partner at a time, although the partnership usually only lasts one year.[28] Larger species and the more sedentary species (like fast-river specialists) tend to have pair-bonds that last numerous years.[29] Most duck species breed once a year, choosing to do so in favou"

slot.instructions: Which words of the transcript are the thing the command carries verbatim: the address to open, the search terms, the song to play, the text to type, the key to press? Never the command word itself: "play X" carries X. A line with no command word, such as a question, carries itself: its search terms are the line as asked. Choose none when it carries none.

options.none: the command carries no words of its own

extent.instructions: Only when the action scrolls the page or a scrolling part of it: how far? Choose words when the words give a number of screens or pages; screen when they say nothing of how far. Ignored for every other action.

options.words: as many screens as the number the words carry
options.little: a little: a third of a screen
options.screen: one screen, as Page Down does
options.end: all the way: to the bottom, or to the top going up

where.instructions: Where do the words point: at something on this page, at something on en.wikipedia.org that is not on this page, or somewhere else on the web?

options.page: on this page: one of the numbered refs
options.site: on en.wikipedia.org but not on this page: a page, a person, a post, a section of it
options.web: elsewhere: another website, or a search of the whole web
